title: US and Iran Target Bridges, Power Plants, and Water Systems as War Enters Infrastructure Phase
excerpt: After seven consecutive nights of US strikes, both sides are hitting civilian infrastructure — bridges in Iran, desalination plants in Kuwait — as the conflict shifts from military targets to essential services.
body:
• The US struck at least five bridges in southern Iran and hit airports and a train station, while Iran retaliated by attacking power plants and water desalination facilities in Kuwait — marking a dangerous shift to infrastructure targeting.
  • Oil prices surged above $86 a barrel, up over 10% for the week, as tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz dropped to two-month lows and Iran declared no oil or gas would leave the region.
  • Iran launched attacks on Saudi Arabia for the first time in approximately three months, hitting near the Prince Sultan Airbase that hosts US forces, and struck military and civilian targets in Kuwait, Bahrain, and Jordan.
  • The UN expressed concern over "attacks on civilian infrastructure in Iran and across the region" as 10,000 people in 20 Iranian villages lost water access after strikes on desalination pumps.

A Week of Escalation

The US-Iran war crossed a significant threshold this past week as both sides expanded their target sets beyond military installations to include bridges, power plants, and water infrastructure. The shift came after the interim ceasefire agreed in June collapsed on July 7, when Iran struck ships in the Strait of Hormuz and Washington responded with air strikes.

US Central Command confirmed it launched its seventh consecutive night of attacks on Friday, saying its targets now include "military logistics infrastructure" — the first time the command mentioned infrastructure in more than a week. Iranian state media reported at least five bridges were struck in southern Iran, with seven people killed in attacks on bridges in the port city of Bandar Khamir. A train station and an airport in Iranshahr were also hit.

"Early warning alarms sounded in Al-Kharj, east of Riyadh, and at Yanbu on the kingdom's Red Sea coast."

Videos verified by Reuters showed rubble, broken railings, and a damaged vehicle on a smashed bridge in Bandar Khamir. The strikes on bridges appeared designed to cut off Iran's Bandar Abbas port — a critical naval and commercial hub — from road connections to Tehran.

Iran Hits Back at Gulf Infrastructure

Iran responded by striking civilian infrastructure across the Gulf. A power generation and water desalination plant in Kuwait was hit, the country's Electricity, Water and Renewable Energy Ministry confirmed — the second attack on Kuwaiti water desalination sites in two days. Kuwait Petroleum Corporation said one of its oil facilities suffered significant damage in "repeated Iranian attacks."

In Iran's southern city of Jask, several missiles struck power facilities and desalination pumps, leaving approximately 10,000 people in 20 villages without water, according to Iran's Tasnim news agency. The governor of Jask later confirmed emergency water deliveries had begun.

Kuwait's Foreign Ministry said Iran's targeting of vital infrastructure endangered civilians and violated international law. The rich Arab Gulf states depend on desalination plants to make their desert cities habitable — when Iran hit a Kuwaiti desalination plant on March 30, it was widely seen as a major escalation.

"Iran and the US are now locked in an escalation spiral, with neither side willing to back down. The war has been costly for Tehran. But its leverage in the strait is valuable — too valuable to give up."

— Bloomberg Economics analysts Becca Wasser and Dina Esfandiary

Saudi Arabia Drawn In

In a notable expansion of the conflict, Iran launched attacks on Saudi Arabia for the first time in about three months, according to two sources cited by Reuters. Early warning alarms sounded in Al-Kharj, east of Riyadh, and at Yanbu on the kingdom's Red Sea coast. One attack targeted the Prince Sultan Airbase in Al-Kharj, which hosts US forces.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards also claimed it attacked a US drone depot in Bahrain and destroyed Bahrain's "main artificial intelligence centre" with ballistic missiles and drones. In Kuwait, operations at Kuwait International Airport were suspended due to repeated missile and drone threats.

Oil Markets and the Strait

Benchmark Brent crude climbed above $86 a barrel on Friday, up more than 10% for the week and nearing its highest level in a month. Iran's Revolutionary Guards declared that until US "aggression" ends, not "a single drop of oil and gas" would leave the region.

Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway through which roughly one-fifth of the world's oil supply passes — has dropped to a three-week low. US Marines boarded a tanker near the strait, while two oil tankers exploded and caught fire after passing through a mined route south of the waterway. Washington has reimposed a blockade of Iranian ports, and Iran has announced the strait's closure to unauthorized traffic.

What It Means for the Indian Diaspora

The infrastructure escalation has direct consequences for Indians in the Gulf. Kuwait's airport suspensions, Saudi Arabia's early warning alarms, and attacks on essential services like water and power affect the estimated 8.5 million Indian nationals living and working across Gulf Cooperation Council states. Rising oil prices threaten India's import bill and are already feeding through into consumer inflation, with transport CPI rebounding to 4.31% in June.

Mohsen Rezaei, an adviser to Iran's supreme leader and former Revolutionary Guards commander, warned: "If US strikes continue for several more days, we will move into a phase of full-scale offensive operations." For now, the UN has called for restraint, but the trajectory is pointing the other way.
